analytic.title: A Method for Dynamic Software Updating in Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: To cope with demands for new and extended functionality, software systems must be updated regularly. This usually requires providing some new codes, merging these codes into the archaic program, and restarting the updated application. This process results in disrupting programs that may be unacceptable, especially in real-time environments which have strict timing constraints. Even, an update which doesn't require the system to stop but causes a deadline to be missed is not a good one in real-time systems. In this paper, we propose a new approach to dynamically update a real-time application without having to disrupt the program. Our method can be applied to update real-time applications in which the rate-monotonic scheduling algorithm is used, while preserving the original deadline guarantees.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Software systems are frequently modified and extended to comply with the changes in requirements and to remove bugs. Before a running program could be modified, it has to be stopped, its source code should be changed, the object code should be re-generated and finally the new version of the program has to be run [12]. However, taking running programs offline due to applying changes is not acceptable in many mission-oriented applications. Even, a banking or telecommunication software system which can't be called a real mission-oriented system, may have prohibitive downtime cost [11].

In addition, mission-oriented applications are often deployed in embedded systems which are mostly real-time [13]. Air Traffic Control System is an example of a missionoriented real-time embedded system which should not be disrupted and, moreover, has to meet predefined deadlines. In such an application, updating should not cause not only the running program to be stopped but also a deadline to be missed or else updating may result in catastrophic consequences.

Precisely speaking, updating should take place on the fly on one hand (i.e. update without stopping which we call it dynamic updating) and it shouldn't cause any deadline to be missed on the other hand (i.e. update with the consideration of timing constraints of real-time systems).

There are plenty of works in dynamic updating [1][4] [6] [9][10] [11] [12], but to the best of our knowledge, only one of them considers timing constraints imposed by real-time systems [10]. This paper like [10] tries to support a real-time system in dynamically updating its tasks.

It's so obvious that the updated version of a task might have different properties from its previous version. For example, the execution time of the updated task very probably differs from that of the replaced task. In the literature, there is no dynamic updating approach for realtime systems which considers this issue yet. In this paper, it's assumed that the new version of task can have a different execution time, a different period or a different deadline.

The original deadline guarantees are preserved via a schedulability test of dynamic updating. The schedulability test proposed here ensures that the system can reply to one update request in each hyper-period while no periodic task misses its deadline. Also, in the worst case, it's guaranteed that the new version of a task is replaced with the old one in the beginning of the next second hyper-period (The hyperperiod after the next hyper-period).

This schedulability test is based on the schedulability test of the RM (Rate Monotonic) scheduling algorithm described in [7]. The reason of choosing RM as the scheduling algorithm is explained later in Section III.A. One more assumption is that update execution time is always constant. As it will be seen in Section III.D, this is a reasonable assumption for many systems.

The remaining parts of this paper are organized as follows: In Section II, we provide a background on previous researches related to our work. Section III describes our new approach for dynamically updating real-time systems and offers some timing guarantees to make the system more predictable. In Section IV, a brief description about the simulation method is provided and then our approach is investigated through some experiments with different workloads. Finally, Section V gives a summary and discusses future directions.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: There has been a wide variety of papers in fault tolerant real-time systems. [3] provides useful ideas in implementing real-time systems with dynamic updating capabilities. Although fault tolerant systems, like dynamic updating systems, can change their behaviors during run-time, they are completely different from our approach in the way of changing behaviors. In fault tolerant real-time systems, all versions of a task should be implemented and integrated into the program before starting it (which is called redundancy), but in our approach new versions of an archaic task should be implemented and integrated during run-time of the program.

In addition, a variety of approaches have been proposed for dynamically updating running software applications. Most of them rely on the support from the run-time system to perform dynamic updates [4] [6] [9], while a few others don't need any further requirements rather than capabilities provided by common programming languages [1] [11] [12].

Although the works in dynamic updating address some issues of updating software applications at run-time, none of them assume timing constraints imposed by real-time systems on running programs. One exception is [10], in which dynamic updating is considered as a transient fault. Since re-scheduling of the new task set has not been desirable for [10], it has assumed that the execution time of the replacement task isn't greater than that of the task it replaces. This assumption is not necessarily true.

div.head: III. DYNAMIC UPDATING OF REAL-TIME TASKS
div.p: In this section, we introduce our approach to dynamic updating. Before diving into our method, let's see a scenario of dynamic updating. Figure 1 shows a snapshot of a realtime system consisting of two tasks, task 1 and task 2. The beginning of each hyper-period is shown with a small vertical line. As it can be seen, a hyper-period of the system begins with starting execution of the 5 th job of task 1 and the next hyper-period begins after finishing execution of the ninth job of task 2.

In addition to task 1 and task 2, another task has been added to the system. We call the set of task 1 and task 2 "original tasks". The other task will be called "dummy" from now on. Note that because of dynamic updating, original tasks are fluctuated over time. Therefore, the original tasks at time t i may be different from the original tasks at time t j .

The main responsibility of dummy task is performing dynamic updating activities. Thus, it should be added to the set of tasks of any real-time system in which dynamic updating capabilities is required. Details of activities which should be done by jobs of dummy task are described in Section III.D. "Dummy" has been chosen for the name of this task because if no update request received in a hyperperiod, its job has nothing to do. In Figure 1, its job has been depicted as a shaded cube. For now, assume that exactly one job of "Dummy" task is executed in each hyper-period and each job needs 6 milliseconds to complete its execution. Determining period and worst case execution time of dummy task is provided in Section III.A and III.D, respectively.

As shown in Figure 1, a request for updating task 1 is received during execution of the fifth job of it. First of all, the system is set so that it won't accept any more update request until next hyper-period arrival and waits for the dummy job to come. After coming, the job of dummy task adds the updated version of task 1 to tasks set and removes its archaic version from tasks of system and then checks to see if the new task set is still schedulable. If the new tasks are not schedulable, the update request is rejected; otherwise, all activities that are related to dynamic updating such as loading the new version of task into memory are performed. However, executing the new version of task 1 instead of the retired one is postponed until the beginning of the next hyper-period. That is, in the execution of the 6 th job of task 1, the old version of this task is still run. Afterwards, the new version of task 1 will be executed. Reasons of this decision have been discussed in Section III.C.

As we saw, the dummy task which is responsible for testing schedulability of tasks and their dynamic updating must exist in each hyper-period. Therefore, it's a periodic task and its execution time and period must be determined. Moreover, since an extra task has been added to the original tasks, schedulability test formulas which have been introduced so far might not work for the system. These are issues that the following sections try to address.

div.head: A. Determining Period of Dummy Task
div.p: To ensure that one dummy task exists in each hyperperiod, it's required to add a task with period equals to the hyper-period of original tasks set. It is clear that adding a task with period equals to the hyper-period of a tasks set doesn't change the hyper-period, because each integer number is dividable by itself. Since no task can have a period greater than the hyper-period, the dummy task has the greatest period and because RM has been chosen as scheduling algorithm, the dummy task has lower priority among tasks. Despite other features of RM such as predictability, the main reason of choosing it as a scheduling algorithm in this paper is to give dummy task the lowest priority without any further modifications of scheduling algorithm. Therefore, it's guaranteed that the dummy job is executed not only in each hyper-period but also as late as possible. The whys of postponing dummy job as late as possible will be cleared in Section III.C. We abstracted the above results in Lemma 1.

div.head: Lemma 1.
div.p: Let the period of the dummy task be equal to the hyper-period of the system task set. Adding the dummy task to the set, it will start its execution at the beginning of the first idle time in the respective schedule. Among all advantages of choosing period of the dummy task equal to the hyper-period of original tasks, this selection has yet another benefit. Since execution time of the dummy task is usually small (Section III.D) and its period has been chosen to be relatively large (because the hyper-period is usually a relatively large number), its utilization is almost small and it doesn't affect schedulability of the original tasks so much.

In this way, we ensure that a job of the dummy task will finally reach and the dynamic updating will not be postponed forever. It is not a restrictive assumption, because a task with the period of infinity can be considered as an aperiodic task and scheduled with another scheduling algorithm in the system. Another important thing that must be noticed is that since dynamic updating may result in changing a task's period and consequently the hyper-period of tasks may be modified, period of the dummy task should be re-calculated each time an update request is received.

div.head: C. Timely Completion of Update
div.p: One important factor in real-time systems is predictability. The exact time after which jobs of archaic task don't run any longer and, in spite of them, the updated jobs start running must be determined.

Since activities of dynamic updating like loading updated task into memory are performed by the nearest dummy job, it seems that the jobs of retired task can be replaced with the updated ones immediately after the completion of the dummy job. However, due to probable changes in the period of the retired task and consequently changes in the hyperperiod, we decided to postpone executing jobs of updated tasks until the beginning of the next hyper-period.

Since the two versions of the updated task may be placed in different memory locations, all of points in the program which use (e.g. call) the updated task should also be updated so that they direct to the new version of the updated task. We call these points as dependent points. Therefore, another activity of each dummy job is finding out and recording the dependent points along with the location of the updated task. Then, at the start of the next hyper-period, these dependent points are updated with the new proper value.

According to the above constraint which restricts the completion of dynamic updating only at the beginning of hyper-periods, and according to lemma 1 which declares that there is just one dummy task in each hyper-period, lemma 2 can be derived.

div.head: Lemma 2. If the final redirection of calls to an updated task is performed only at the beginning of hyper-periods, then in the worst case, it's guaranteed that the old version of the task is replaced with the new one at the start of the next second hyper-period.
div.p: In order to show the correctness of lemma 2, we consider two different cases of update request arrival which can occur. It is clear that every update request is received in a hyperperiod, but it can be received (1) before the execution of the dummy task in that hyper-period or (2) after the execution of the dummy task in that hyper-period. These two cases are shown in Figure 2.

In case 1, the dummy job of the hyper-period in which update request is received, performs dynamic updating activities. Thus, jobs of the updated task can be executed from the beginning of the next hyper-period. In case 2, since the dummy job of the hyper-period in which update request is received has formerly started its execution, update request should wait for dummy job of the next hyper-period. At the starting point, the dummy job performs dynamic updating activities and jobs of the updated task can be executed from the beginning of the next second hyper-period.

As it has been shown, in the worst case, the dynamic updating is finished at the beginning of the next second hyper-period. However, if the execution of the dummy job is postponed as late as possible in each hyper-period, probability of receiving an update request before running of the dummy job in that hyper-period becomes higher. In other words, most of the times, case 1 of the above discussion occurs and therefore, the dynamic updating is finished one hyper-period sooner. This is why we desire to assign the lowest possible priority to the dummy task.

div.head: D. Determining Activities of Dummy Ttask
div.p: In this subsection, we exactly list activities that should be performed during dynamic updating. This can help us describe our idea as an algorithm. Furthermore, since these activities are the responsibility of the dummy task, the execution time of the dummy task, C update , can also be estimated. The following is the list of activities which should be performed by the dummy job if an update request has been received: 1. Set state of the system to "Updating". 2. Create a temporary set of tasks, S temp , with the following elements:

Add a dummy task, T dummy new , to the tasks set S temp . Note that the task's period is the hyper-period calculated in step 3 and its execution time is C update . In other words, S temp = S temp ∪ { T dummy new }. 5. Check to see if tasks of the temporary set, S temp , are schedulable. If not, reject the request, set state of the system to "Running" and exit. 6. Load new version of the updated task into memory.
Also, store memory address of the updated task to Loc updated . 7. Find and record address of dependent points in the application which use the task being updated.
Then, the following activities should be performed at the beginning of each hyper-period:

1. If state of the system is "Running" exit. 2. Update the points found in step 7 of the above algorithm so that they direct to Loc updated , from now on. 3. Set S = S temp . 4. Set state of the system to "Running" Although the detailed steps that should be performed by every dummy job have been shown here, calculating the exact worst case execution time (WCET) of the dummy task isn't trivial at all [8]. However, there are tools available for calculating the worst case execution time of programs. [5] and [2] have proposed two of the most popular kinds of such tools, Volta and aiT, respectively. However, none of today WCET analyzers are suitable for determining the worst case execution time of dynamic updating; because (1) almost all of these tools require some user inputs such as loop bounds to work precisely and (2) they don't predict the execution time of any I/O operation while step 6 of the dummy task is an I/O operation.

In spite of the above realities, a quick glance at the steps of the dummy task shows that step 6 needs much longer (about 1000 times longer) time than the other steps to run, because it's the only I/O operation among the steps. So, the other steps execution time is negligible. In addition, according to the literature, each I/O operation takes a few milliseconds (3ms -7ms) to complete. Therefore, we assume the worst case execution time of the dummy task is 6 milliseconds for the time being. The work is going on to make our assumption more precise.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In order to evaluate our work, we studied the behavior of a real-time system which can dynamically update its tasks using the approach proposed in this paper. The study was performed with a simulation application written by the same authors with Java 1.6.

The simulation application gets an initial tasks set from the user and then starts two running threads. The first thread executes jobs of defined tasks and records every event that occurs in the system while the second thread receives update requests from the user. The user can obtain any report he/she likes from the output files that the simulation generates.

The other application was written to generate a desirable number of tasks sets and update requests to inject them to the simulation application. We use these two threads to measure the number of accepted and/or rejected update requests in different workloads. For this purpose, the following parameters were given to the system: The result is shown in Table I. As it can be seen, the number of accepted or rejected update requests is almost independent of workload. As the last column of Table I shows, another significant result is that the constraint described in Lemma 2 doesn't cause to reject unreasonable number of update requests. For example, for workload of 0.750, no update request has been rejected for the constraint incurred by our approach.

V. CONCLUSIONS Our main goal in this paper was to dynamically update tasks without any presumption about tasks' periods and execution times. In other words, period or execution time of an updated task can be less than, equal to, or greater than its previous one. Some lemmas and formulas are provided to guarantee against (1) the schedulability of the system with dynamic updating capabilities and (2) the completion time of dynamic updating. In addition, a system which can dynamically update tasks using the ideas of this paper has been simulated. Then, the idea was evaluated by measuring the number of rejected update requests because of the idea's constraints.

In this work, the update request should wait 2 hyperperiods in the worst cases. Work is ongoing to make the time of dynamic updating shorter in the worst circumstances. Another work-in-progress in our model is to determine the worst case execution time of the dummy task more precisely. In general, it's so critical to have precise worst case execution times in real-time systems while it is not a trivial task at all.
